title: You Know Everybody Else’s Theology. When Did Knowing Jesus Become Secondary?
paragraphs:
You Know Everybody Else’s Theology. When Did Knowing Jesus Become Secondary?
You can identify bad doctrine in seconds, defend the faith for hours, and explain what everybody else gets wrong. But when knowledge makes us easier to impress with ourselves and harder to recognize as people who have been with Jesus, something sacred has gone terribly wrong.
There is a frightening way to be right about God…
and slowly become unlike Him.
You know the verses.
You know the doctrines.
You know the debates.

You know which preacher mishandled the text, which denomination you disagree with, which theological system has holes in it, which translation you prefer, which interpretation you reject, which church movement concerns you, and which Greek word everybody on Facebook apparently misunderstood.
Someone posts a theological statement, and before you finish reading it, your mind is already preparing the correction.
You know everybody else’s theology.
But here is the question that may hurt more than any doctrinal argument:
When did knowing Jesus become secondary?
Not knowing about Jesus.
Knowing Him.
Loving Him.
Worshiping Him.
Obeying Him when obedience costs something.
Sitting before His Word without needing to prove that you already understand it.
Repenting when Scripture exposes you instead of immediately thinking about somebody else who needs to read it.
Becoming gentler because Christ has been gentle with you.
Becoming slower to condemn because you remember how much mercy it took to rescue you.
Becoming holy because the One you study has become the One you treasure.
Paul confronted something painfully similar in Corinth.

The immediate controversy involved food sacrificed to idols. Some Corinthian Christians possessed legitimate theological knowledge. They understood truths about idols and about God that mattered. Paul did not solve the problem by declaring theology irrelevant.
Instead, he exposed what knowledge can become when the heart holding it is no longer governed by love.
In 1 Corinthians 8:1, Paul writes:
ἡ γνῶσις φυσιοῖ, ἡ δὲ ἀγάπη οἰκοδομεῖ.
Hē gnōsis physioi, hē de agapē oikodomei.
In context, the sense is:
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”
Look at those words.
γνῶσις — gnōsis — knowledge.
φυσιοῖ — physioi — puffs up, inflates.
ἀγάπη — agapē — love.
οἰκοδομεῖ — oikodomei — builds up, edifies.
Paul is not saying knowledge is evil.
He is showing us what knowledge can do when it becomes disconnected from love.
It can inflate.
That image should disturb every serious student of Scripture.
Because inflation creates the appearance of enlargement without necessarily creating corresponding substance.
And that means you can become larger in your own eyes while becoming smaller in love.
You can increase your theological vocabulary while decreasing your patience.
You can memorize more Scripture while becoming less merciful toward people who are still learning it.
You can understand justification and still secretly justify your arrogance.
You can defend sovereign grace while behaving as though your superior intelligence saved you.
You can explain sanctification while refusing to repent.
You can study the humility of Christ and become proud of how accurately you understand His humility.
That last one should frighten us.
Because spiritual pride can feed on almost anything.
Even truth.
Especially truth, when we forget that truth is something we received before it was something we mastered.
Somewhere along the journey, Bible study can quietly stop being a place where we meet God and become a place where we collect ammunition.
The Scriptures become weapons for winning arguments rather than a sword first permitted to pierce our own hearts.
We begin reading with other people in mind.
“This verse is exactly what they need.”
“This destroys their position.”
“This proves our side.”
“This pastor needs to hear this.”
“This denomination needs to repent.”
“This person clearly hasn't studied enough.”
Maybe sometimes those concerns are legitimate.
False teaching is real.
Doctrine matters profoundly.
The New Testament repeatedly calls believers to discern truth, guard the Gospel, resist deception, teach faithfully, and grow in understanding.
Christian love is not intellectual laziness.
And biblical humility does not require pretending every interpretation is equally faithful to Scripture.
But there is another danger that serious Christians sometimes find harder to detect:
You can become skilled at discovering error everywhere except in yourself.
Paul continues:
εἴ τις δοκεῖ ἐγνωκέναι τι, οὔπω ἔγνω καθὼς δεῖ γνῶναι.
Ei tis dokei egnōkenai ti, oupō egnō kathōs dei gnōnai.
The thought of 1 Corinthians 8:2 is devastating:
If someone imagines that he knows something, he has not yet known as he ought to know.
Read that slowly.
Paul is confronting the arrogance that says,
“I know.”
Not humble confidence in revealed truth.
Not conviction.
Not careful doctrine.
But the posture that has stopped being teachable because it has become impressed with itself.
And then Paul turns the entire conversation toward something deeper:
εἰ δέ τις ἀγαπᾷ τὸν θεόν, οὗτος ἔγνωσται ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ.
Ei de tis agapa ton theon, houtos egnōstai hyp’ autou.
“But if anyone loves God, he is known by Him.”
Suddenly the center of gravity changes.
The ultimate wonder of Christianity is not that you have accumulated information about God.
It is that, by grace, God knows you.
You belong to Him.
You have been called into fellowship with His Son.
Christianity was never supposed to terminate in your ability to explain Christianity.
Theology is meant to lead somewhere.
To wonder.
To worship.
To obedience.
To love.
To holiness.
To communion with the living Christ.
The goal is not to know less theology.
The goal is to know God so truly that what you know begins transforming the person who knows it.
That distinction matters.
Because sound doctrine is precious.
We desperately need it.
A church without truth becomes vulnerable to every spiritual counterfeit wearing Christian vocabulary.
But doctrine was never given to us as a throne from which we could look down upon everyone who knows less.
It was given as light leading sinners toward the glory of God revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to become painfully honest.
When was the last time studying Scripture made you weep?
Not because the interpretation was fascinating.
Because Jesus became beautiful again.
When was the last time you closed your Bible and needed to repent?
When was the last time you discovered something true about God and your first impulse was worship rather than posting?
When was the last time your theology made you more patient with the immature believer?
More compassionate toward the struggling Christian?
More burdened for the unbeliever?
More forgiving toward the person who wounded you?
More willing to serve where nobody applauds?
More aware of your dependence upon grace?
When was the last time knowing more made you feel smaller before the majesty of God rather than larger beside other Christians?
Because there is a difference between theological maturity and theological accumulation.
Accumulation can fill notebooks.
Maturity changes people.
Accumulation can win debates.
Maturity knows when winning the person matters more than displaying the argument.
Accumulation can quote Christ.
Maturity increasingly resembles Him.
And then we come to Jesus Himself.
The One about whom all our Christology speaks.
The One whose nature we debate.
The One whose atonement we defend.
The One whose resurrection we proclaim.
The One whose return we await.
Look at Him.
Jesus knew every Scripture perfectly.
He never misunderstood the Father.
He never held an incorrect doctrine.
He never needed correction.
Absolute truth stood in human flesh.
And what did perfect knowledge look like when it walked among sinners?
It touched lepers.
It welcomed children.
It confronted hypocrisy.
It defended truth.
It wept.
It served.
It washed feet.
It called sinners to repentance.
It showed compassion to the broken.
And then…
it carried a cross.
There is your theology with skin on it.
Jesus Christ did not become less truthful in order to become loving.
And He did not become less loving in order to remain truthful.
In Him, grace and truth are not enemies.
At Calvary, the holiness of God was not discarded.
Sin was not renamed.
Judgment was not treated as imaginary.
The cross tells us sin is far worse than our culture wants to believe.
But it also tells us grace is far greater than religious pride wants to admit.
The Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Not people who had finally accumulated enough theological precision to deserve Him.
Sinners.
Rebels.
The guilty.
People with ruined histories.
People who misunderstood.
People who failed.
People who hid.
People who promised loyalty and then collapsed under pressure.
People like Peter.
People like the Corinthians.
People like us.
That is the scandal.
And then comes grace.
Jesus takes people whose sin should have been the final chapter and begins writing something new.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming what sin tried to destroy.
This is why the Gospel destroys both intellectual arrogance and intellectual laziness.
We cannot say truth does not matter, because Christ is the truth.
But we cannot boast as though understanding truth makes us superior, because everything we possess is grace.
The cross leaves no room for swagger.
You did not save yourself.
Your systematic theology did not bleed for you.
Your favorite teacher did not rise from the grave for you.
Your denomination cannot wash away your sin.
Your apologetics cannot reconcile you to God.
Your knowledge cannot justify you.
Jesus saves.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And when that truth moves from the edges back to the center, something happens.
The Bible student becomes a worshiper again.
The debater remembers that the person on the other side of the screen has a soul.
The teacher trembles before teaching.
The mature believer remembers how patient somebody once had to be with them.
Correction becomes less about humiliation and more about restoration.
Conviction becomes less performative.
Repentance becomes personal.
Truth remains truth.
But pride starts losing oxygen.
Maybe that is why this article feels uncomfortable.
Perhaps you have not abandoned Jesus.
Perhaps something subtler happened.
You became fascinated with everything surrounding Him…
and stopped being fascinated with Him.
You know the controversies.
You know the camps.
You know the terminology.
You know everybody who is supposedly wrong.
But somewhere beneath all that knowledge is a heart that remembers when simply hearing the name Jesus could undo you.
When grace amazed you.
When the cross felt personal.
When salvation was not merely a doctrine you could define but a miracle you could barely believe had happened to you.
When you opened Scripture hungry rather than armed.
Maybe you miss that person.
Maybe Christ is calling you away from the exhausting need to prove that you belong among the knowledgeable and back into the joy of simply belonging to Him.
That does not mean throwing away serious theology.
It means putting theology back where it belongs:
At the feet of Jesus.
Study harder.
Read carefully.
Learn biblical languages if you can.
Understand church history.
Test teachings against Scripture.
Know why you believe what you believe.
Protect the Gospel.
Teach sound doctrine.
Refuse counterfeit Christianity.
But never become so impressed with knowing things about God that you forget the terrifying, beautiful privilege of actually knowing Him.

And whenever knowledge begins making you cruel, suspiciously proud, contemptuous, unteachable, addicted to controversy, or incapable of loving the people for whom Christ died, do not congratulate yourself for being discerning.
Bring your heart back under the Word.
Let Scripture examine the examiner.
Let truth correct the person correcting everybody else.
Repent.
Because repentance is not intellectual defeat.
Repentance is one of grace's greatest victories.
Maybe your scandal was never the kind people whisper about.
Maybe yours was quieter.
Nobody saw it.
You became proud.
You started needing to be the smartest Christian in the room.
You began measuring spiritual maturity by how much somebody agreed with you.
You forgot that knowledge is stewardship.
You forgot that the person you corrected was a person.
You forgot your own rescue.
And perhaps Jesus is rewriting that story too.
From pride to humility.
From argument to worship.
From merely knowing propositions about Christ to walking closely with Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
Someone reading may pray for you instead of judging you.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought, and salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
But if Gospel-centered teaching has genuinely strengthened you, supporting work that spreads biblical truth can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
Your share may place the Gospel in front of the person who would never walk into a church but will quietly read something a friend posted at 2:00 in the morning.
Your tag may reach the Christian who has become exhausted by religious performance.
Your comment may give another believer permission to stop hiding.
Your support can help Gospel-centered material keep moving.

It is an opportunity to help sustain and expand Gospel-centered discipleship while receiving deeper biblical nourishment, encouragement, accountability, and resources designed to keep pointing you toward Christ.
Jesus is not for sale.
The blood of Christ cannot be purchased.
Come to Him empty-handed.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Then spend the rest of your life learning the truth—not so you can stand taller than other sinners, but so you can bow lower before the Savior.
Because one day, nobody will be impressed that you won every theological argument.
The question underneath all the questions will remain:
Did all that truth lead you deeper into Christ?
Did knowing more make you love Him more?
Did it make you obey Him?
Did it make you worship?
Did it make you love the people He loves?
Did it make you look more like Jesus?
Never become so knowledgeable about the Light that you forget to stand in it.
